Chapter 6

# Climate change and migration: understanding the context 

### Main characteristics

The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report and the World Meteorological Organization 13 both emphasize that climate change impacts are intensifying globally, affecting where people settle and contributing to increased pressure to move.

Climate change is reshaping human mobility through both sudden-onset hazards (e.g. floods, storms, wildfires) and slow-onset changes (e.g. drought, rising sea levels), which have different impacts on climate mobility. Sudden-onset events trigger large-scale, rapid and predominantly forced movements that are mostly short term and short distance but can become protracted if recovery is delayed or repeated hazards occur. In contrast, slow-onset changes like coastal erosion or land degradation may lead to more diverse mobility outcomes: short or long term, individual or group based, internal or cross-border. A decision to move, however, is usually a result of an interplay of multiple considerations, where climate change pressures often intersect with economic, social and political factors and other drivers of migration. 14 Made at an individual or household level, or in some cases at a community level, such decisions are influenced by perceptions of risk, social networks, wealth, age structure, health and livelihood choices and, importantly, perceived alternatives to moving. 15 Therefore, the same environmental change can have different human mobility implications for different social groups and individuals, at different times and in different locations.

This causal complexity means that it is difficult to weight the impact of climate change or any other single factor in shaping mobility outcomes. Another implication of the complexity is that there is no single form of human mobility that can be attributed to climate change; instead, the full spectrum of migration patterns can be linked to climate change impacts – from voluntary to forced, within and across borders, temporary, circular or permanent. At the same time, most climate-related mobility occurs within countries, frequently from rural areas into towns and cities; and cross-border flows usually remain regional. 16 This variety and multicausality mean that migration and displacement in climate change contexts can produce different outcomes for migrants and affected societies, both negative and positive. How people move and their agency in the process are among the key factors influencing what impacts mobility has on individuals and societies. In some cases, people move because they have no choice – moving away from a disaster zone can be lifesaving. Such a move can take different forms, from disaster displacement to planned relocation. It may be initiated by governments or communities, and is often associated with complex social and ethical challenges. Forced movement, whether within a country or across a border, often brings hardship and suffering, including exposure to an array of human rights violations. Whether triggered by slow- or sudden-onset hazards, displacement aggravates pre-existing patterns of discrimination and abuse. In the context of international movements, irregular migration is another significant factor increasing the vulnerability of people on the move to human rights violations, violence and exploitation. On the other hand, well-managed migration can be a positive adaptation strategy, helping migrants and their communities become more resilient in the face of climate change. 17 

Another important dimension of the climate change and migration nexus is the issue of involuntary immobility. 18 Migration requires economic and other resources, and therefore it is not an option open to everyone. Climate change impacts not only drive migration but can also make it more difficult or even impossible for some individuals or groups to move. It is such “trapped populations” 19 and individuals who face the gravest risks from climate change impacts.

This complexity points to the need for nuanced, multipronged approaches to climate-related mobility that address underlying socioeconomic issues and vulnerabilities and are context specific. Local-level action is well suited to designing and implementing such solutions. Before turning to these responses, and to how local actors can implement them more effectively, the next section briefly examines the availability and quality of data and evidence, the essential foundation for planning and for effective responses to diverse patterns of climate-related mobility.

### The knowledge base and knowledge gaps

The knowledge base on links between climate change and human mobility is significant, though uneven. It is grounded in a growing body of evidence drawn from diverse disciplines, combining quantitative data with qualitative field research, environmental and socioeconomic indicators, and localized case studies. This section provides a brief overview of what the current data reveal and the main gaps, from global patterns to local insights.

Global level data and analysis

Despite significant progress made in recent years, the global data on the effects of environmental changes on migration and displacement remain limited in several important ways. While there is a solid understanding of the anticipated biophysical effects of climate change, much uncertainty remains regarding how human mobility patterns will be influenced by these changes. 20 This is due in part to the complexity, mentioned above, of the relationship between climate impacts and human mobility. So, though “most statistical models indicate that certain climate-related factors have some effect on migration … there is no consensus on how strong that effect is or, in some cases, even whether the effect is positive or negative.” 21 

There are global data available on particular dimensions of climate-related human mobility. There are, for example, more and better data on forced movements triggered by sudden-onset disasters (see the box on internal climate displacement). However, data on other important dimensions of climate mobility – such as slow-onset impacts, 22 local-level dynamics and marginalized and vulnerable populations – remain limited.

Key figures: spotlight on internal climate displacement

Since 2008, storms, floods, droughts and wildfires triggered 401.6 million internal displacements worldwide. a These hazards occurred in all parts of the world but were unequally distributed. Figure 1 illustrates displacement in 2024 by geographic location and type of weather hazard.

##### Figure 1. Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre records of weather-related internal displacements in 2024

 Source: Authors' elaboration based on IDMC data (IDMC, n.d.). Notes: This map is for illustration purposes only. The boundaries and names shown and the designations used on this map do not imply official endorsement or acceptance by IOM. 

In 2024, there were 45.8 million new internal displacements triggered by disasters, mostly by storms (25.2 million) and floods (19.1 million). b These displacements occurred across 163 countries and territories. Moreover, an estimated 9.8 million people were internally displaced due to disasters at the end of the same year. East Asia and the Pacific and the Americas recorded the highest overall number of disaster displacements globally. c Countries such as the United States, the Philippines and India had some of the largest number of displacements. d 

Women and girls constitute a significant share of disaster-related displacements, with many displacements occurring in countries already ranked in the bottom quartile of the Gender Inequality Index. e This amplifies risks that displaced women are disproportionally exposed to, such as disrupted reproductive health services and gender-based violence.

Global projections of future climate-related migration and displacement is another actively explored area with multiple studies dedicated to this topic over the years. While most studies anticipate that climate change will increase migration globally, some point to scenarios where international migration will be constrained, especially for low-income groups, due to climate change impacts, resulting in increased “immobility”. 23 There is a significant variation in the scale of the expected impact, as challenges of capturing the full range of implications of climate change for human mobility are further compounded by uncertainties, such as those concerning future emissions and demographic shifts. The range of existing projections for 2050 is vast – from 143 million to 1.2 billion people (Figure 2 illustrates the range of estimates for climate migration and their sources). 24

Notes: This chart illustrates frequently cited projections of climate change-induced migration; the scope of movement these projections cover and the global warming scenarios vary.

Several models have been developed to forecast how climate change will affect human mobility in the future, but inconsistencies in scope and definitions, as well as regional focuses, make direct comparisons difficult. 25 Some approaches focus on estimating small-scale processes over short-time horizons. Others take a broader view over longer periods of time in order to illustrate the range of possible opportunities, challenges and responses.

IOM, for example, uses data modelling to identify areas where environmental stressors intersect with other key drivers of migration to help target resources and inform action. The Migration Data Portal includes an interactive climate mobility impacts dashboard, 26 visualizing projected overlaps between hazard exposure, high population density and economic vulnerability, which are key factors influencing climate-related migration. The dashboard allows users to explore future global hotspots and human exposure to climate impacts across time and under different climatic and socioeconomic scenarios (see Figure 3 for an illustration).

For a more nuanced picture, IOM carries out regional and country level analyses (e.g. Bangladesh, Haiti and Somalia). This modelling uses real-time data and vulnerability indicators to highlight “mobility hotspots” at the community or regional level.

A recent review of climate-related forecasting models points to locally focused agent-based simulations of household and community behaviour, together with statistical extrapolations of observed mobility patterns, as offering the most decision-relevant insights. It also stresses the need for transdisciplinary collaboration to refine forecasts. 27 Overall, whether looking at the current situation or anticipating the future, global figures, while informative, do not reflect the complex, context-specific factors influencing climate-related mobility, such as vulnerability, governance structures and social dynamics. These factors are better captured at the local level. 28
